strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practical challenge in simulation-based inference (SBI): the prohibitive computational cost of running high-fidelity simulators for parameter inference.
The proposed transfer learning strategy is intuitive, simple to implement, and directly compatible with standard modern SBI pipelines (such as Neural Spline Flows).

The method is validated not only on an analytical toy problem (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process) but also on two challenging, realistic neuroscience problems (a multicompartmental Hodgkin-Huxley single neuron model and a 24-parameter plastic recurrent spiking neural network).
The paper clearly explains how to handle dimensional mismatch between the low-fidelity and high-fidelity parameter spaces by introducing dummy variables during pre-training.
weaknesses: Conceptual and algorithmic novelty is limited. The core contribution (MF-NPE) is essentially standard pre-training of a normalizing flow on low-fidelity simulation data followed by fine-tuning on high-fidelity simulation data, without domain-specific algorithmic or architectural innovations.

Important multifidelity baselines are missing. For example, a straightforward baseline would be joint training with a fidelity indicator/conditioning variable (i.e., learning $q_\phi(\theta | x, fidelity)$ across combined LF and HF datasets) or multi-task learning, which are standard in surrogate and multifidelity modeling.

The sequential active learning extension (A-MF-TSNPE) yields minimal empirical improvement over MF-TSNPE (as acknowledged in Section 4.1) while adding noticeable computational overhead (ensembling) and introducing an uncorrected proposal bias that compromises exactness.

There is a lack of systematic investigation into the impact of the fidelity gap or misspecification between the LF and HF models. The risk of negative transfer when the LF model is poorly aligned or misleading is only briefly discussed in the text rather than empirically or theoretically analyzed.

The dimensionality of inferred parameters remains relatively low for two of the three tasks (4 parameters for OU, 2 parameters for the single neuron model), leaving the scalability of the dummy-variable approach to larger dimensional discrepancies less thoroughly tested.

strengths: Addresses a crucial bottleneck in simulation-based inference (SBI): the heavy computational expense of high-fidelity simulators, which often prevents SBI from being applied to realistic scientific problems.
The proposed transfer learning framework (MF-NPE) and its sequential extension (MF-TSNPE) are conceptually straightforward, practical, and easy to integrate into existing SBI pipelines.

The empirical evaluation includes compelling domain applications in neuroscience (a biophysically detailed multicompartmental neuron model and a 24-parameter plastic recurrent spiking network with a mean-field low-fidelity model), demonstrating substantial sample efficiency gains in low high-fidelity simulation regimes.

The paper is clearly written, well-organized, and provides useful diagnostic evaluations including classifier two-sample tests (C2ST), posterior predictive checks, and simulation-based calibration (SBC).
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is somewhat incremental, as the core approach amounts to standard transfer learning (pre-training a neural density estimator on low-fidelity data and fine-tuning on high-fidelity data) within existing NPE/TSNPE frameworks.

The handling of parameter space mismatches (when the low-fidelity model has fewer parameters than the high-fidelity model) relies on a basic dummy-variable strategy; while functional, a deeper methodological investigation or comparison with architectural adaptations is lacking.

The active learning extension (A-MF-TSNPE) yields negligible performance gains over MF-TSNPE in the experiments (as acknowledged by the authors in Section 4.1) while adding significant compute and ensembling overhead, and is not evaluated on the neuroscience benchmarks.

Baselines are limited exclusively to standard single-fidelity NPE/TSNPE. A comparison or discussion against existing multi-fidelity likelihood-free / surrogate-based approaches (e.g., multifidelity ABC or Gaussian process surrogate SBI) would strengthen the empirical grounding.

The paper lacks an explicit wall-clock time or total compute budget frontier (accounting for low-fidelity data generation and pre-training overhead alongside high-fidelity simulation cost) to quantify the net efficiency trade-off across varying simulation costs.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical challenge in simulation-based inference (SBI): leveraging inexpensive low-fidelity approximations to reduce the simulation budget needed for costly high-fidelity simulators.
The proposed transfer learning formulation is straightforward, flexible, and easy to integrate into standard neural posterior estimation (NPE) pipelines.

Evaluation includes realistic, computationally heavy applications in neuroscience (multicompartmental single neurons and recurrent spiking networks with plasticity), rather than purely synthetic toy benchmarks.
The paper provides a practical heuristic for handling mismatched parameter spaces between low- and high-fidelity models by utilizing dummy variables during pre-training.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core contribution (MF-NPE) is essentially standard pre-training and fine-tuning applied to a normalizing flow density estimator, while MF-TSNPE is a direct warm-start of TSNPE.

The active learning variant (A-MF-TSNPE) lacks theoretical rigor; injecting samples selected via ensemble variance into the proposal without importance weighting or density correction introduces bias into the posterior estimation. Moreover, empirical gains over standard MF-TSNPE are negligible despite significant additional computational overhead.

The sequential and active learning variants (MF-TSNPE and A-MF-TSNPE) are only evaluated on the toy Ornstein-Uhlenbeck task and omitted from the two realistic neuroscience experiments, leaving their utility in complex settings unvalidated.

Lack of comparison with existing multifidelity likelihood-free baselines (e.g., multifidelity ABC or Gaussian process surrogate-assisted methods) to contextualize the trade-offs of the deep density estimation approach.

The accounting of computational cost is incomplete: the primary comparisons focus strictly on the number of high-fidelity simulations without adequately characterizing total wall-clock time or cumulative compute trade-offs (including low-fidelity data generation and two-stage neural network training).

strengths: Addresses a crucial bottleneck in simulation-based inference (SBI): the prohibitive computational cost of high-fidelity mechanistic simulators.

Strong and convincing real-world application to neuroscience problems (a multicompartmental biophysical neuron model simulated with Jaxley and a 24-parameter recurrent spiking network with synaptic plasticity simulated with Auryn paired with a mean-field low-fidelity model).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation covering standard benchmark tasks (SIR, SLCP, Gaussian Blob, OU process) and demonstrating significant reduction in high-fidelity simulation budgets (often by 1–2 orders of magnitude).

Insightful analysis of when low-fidelity pre-training succeeds (Section 4.4 and Appendix B), demonstrating through controlled experiments that both mutual information and representational coherence are essential for successful transfer.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty of MF-NPE is relatively modest, consisting primarily of standard transfer learning (pre-training a normalizing flow on low-fidelity pairs and fine-tuning on high-fidelity pairs).

A-MF-TSNPE introduces an asymptotic bias: as acknowledged in Appendix M.2, adding actively acquired samples ($B = 0.2M$) without proposal/density ratio correction biases the proposal distribution away from the TSNPE truncation guarantee, potentially compromising calibration.

The active learning extension (A-MF-TSNPE) provides marginal empirical gain over MF-TSNPE on several benchmark tasks (e.g., SLCP and SIR in Figure 2) despite incurring substantial computational overhead from training an ensemble of neural flows.

Comparisons to other modern simulation-efficient SBI baselines (e.g., surrogate-assisted SBI like SNRE/SNPE with surrogate simulators, or active learning SBI methods like Griesemer et al., 2024) are missing, focusing primarily on standard NPE, TSNPE, and MF-ABC.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical bottleneck in simulation-based inference (SBI), where high-fidelity simulators are often too computationally expensive for standard neural posterior estimation approaches.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning standard synthetic SBI benchmarks (SLCP, SIR, OU process, Gaussian Blob) as well as two realistic, high-dimensional computational neuroscience applications (multicompartmental neuron model and plastic spiking network).
Demonstrates substantial simulation efficiency gains, often matching the accuracy of baseline NPE/TSNPE with one to two orders of magnitude fewer high-fidelity simulator calls.
The handling of parameter dimension mismatch between low- and high-fidelity simulators via dummy variable conditioning is pragmatic and empirically effective.
Insightful analysis in Section 4.4 and Appendix B exploring the conditions under which pre-training succeeds, showing that both mutual information and representational coherence are critical.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is relatively modest, as MF-NPE primarily amounts to standard warm-starting/fine-tuning of Normalizing Flows from low-fidelity to high-fidelity datasets, built on top of the existing TSNPE framework.

In A-MF-TSNPE, pooling samples selected via the active acquisition function directly into the proposal dataset without importance weight or proposal correction introduces an uncorrected bias into the density estimator, which is only addressed via a heuristic ratio (B = 0.2M).

The active variant (A-MF-TSNPE) provides inconsistent benefits over standard MF-TSNPE (e.g., showing no significant gains on SLCP or SIR) while incurring a substantial training computational overhead from maintaining an ensemble of flows.

The approach strictly relies on domain-specific access to a low-fidelity model that shares observation spaces (or easily mapable statistics) with the high-fidelity simulator, which may not always be available in practice.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical bottleneck in simulation-based inference (SBI): modern high-fidelity mechanistic simulators are often computationally prohibitive, making standard sample-hungry neural posterior estimation impractical.

Compelling evaluation on realistic and complex scientific simulators, specifically a multicompartmental biophysical neuron model (using Jaxley) and a 24-parameter plastic recurrent spiking neural network with a mean-field low-fidelity surrogate (using Auryn).
Consistently demonstrates substantial reductions in required high-fidelity simulations (often 1–2 orders of magnitude) across several benchmarks and metrics (C2ST, MMD, NLTP, NRMSE, and SBC).
Provides a simple yet functional approach for handling parameter mismatch when the low-fidelity simulator operates on a lower-dimensional parameter subspace via dummy parameter initialization.
Includes thoughtful diagnostic experiments (Section 4.4 and Appendix B) probing when transfer learning succeeds or fails as a function of mutual information and representational coherence.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is relatively incremental, essentially adapting standard transfer learning (pre-training on low-fidelity data and fine-tuning on high-fidelity data) to neural spline flows within NPE and TSNPE.

The active learning extension (A-MF-TSNPE) introduces an uncorrected heuristic: mixing 20% active samples chosen via predictive variance into the TSNPE proposal violates the importance sampling / proposal truncation guarantees and introduces asymptotic bias, which is only informally addressed.

A-MF-TSNPE provides mixed empirical improvements (showing noticeable gains on OU process, but marginal to no significant improvement on SLCP and SIR) while requiring an ensemble of flows that multiplies training compute by roughly 5x.

The evaluation predominantly treats low-fidelity simulation cost as negligible; a more systematic study of joint computational budget allocation (balancing high-fidelity simulations, low-fidelity simulations, and neural network training costs) is left for future work.
